question.text: Mr. Sanjay Raghavan manages a Cayman-domiciled offshore fund with Indian origin LPs from his office in Mumbai. To ensure that the offshore fund does NOT create an Indian tax residence or business connection merely because its manager operates from India, which provision of the ITA does he rely on, and what is its scope?

answer.text: Section 115UB — the standard AIF pass-through, extended to offshore funds managed from India.
Section 194LBB — a withholding safe harbour that exempts offshore-managed funds from TDS.
Section 10(23FBA) — exempts offshore fund income at fund level.

Section 9A — a safe harbour that, subject to specified conditions, prevents the offshore fund from being treated as an Indian resident or as having a business connection in India solely due to the fund manager being located in India.

explanation.text: The Logic: Section 9A of the ITA provides a statutory safe harbour for eligible offshore investment funds managed by an eligible Indian-based fund manager. Subject to conditions (fund residency, broad-based investors, independence of manager, arm's-length remuneration, diversification tests etc.), the fund is NOT treated as Indian tax resident merely because the manager is in India, and the manager's activities do NOT create a business connection under Section 9. This is the policy cornerstone for onshoring fund management talent. The Trap: Option A is a different section entirely — 115UB covers domestic Cat I/II AIFs. Option C invents a TDS safe harbour that doesn't exist. Option D is the exemption provision for non-business income of domestic Cat I/II AIFs, not offshore fund managers. Cross-Exam Context: XIX-C tests Sec 9A as the fund-manager-domicile carve-out. XIX-E (Cat III) will test Sec 9A because many offshore hedge-style funds use it. X-B (IA L2) touches on it for cross-border structuring. The GIFT IFSC version of Sec 9A has been progressively liberalised to attract managers. Manager's Pro-Tip: If your Cat II fund is planning a GIFT-IFSC offshore sleeve, map each Sec 9A condition against the PPM and mandate well before launch. The 'broad-basing' test (25 investors, single-investor 10% cap) is a frequent trip-wire — build it into subscription agreements rather than retrofitting later.
